title: Graph Intelligence: Enhance Reasoning and Retrieval Using Graph Analytics - Alison & Andreas, Neo4j
talk_summary: Neo4j talk shows how to build and analyze a graph of application activity plus document chunks, then use graph algorithms such as KNN, community detection, PageRank, co-occurrence, and node collapse to curate retrieval context. It is mostly RAG/knowledge-graph guidance, but several mechanisms transfer to agent context/memory and review pipelines.

takeaways.what_they_do: They model sessions, user prompts, assistant responses, and retrieved context documents as one connected graph, then analyze which documents are used and how conversations move.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I call it the application graph. Like they call it a memory graph.

takeaways.technique: Cluster embeddings to curate and dedupe context
takeaways.what_they_do: They run KNN similarity on document embeddings, then community detection to group near-duplicates and inspect cluster-level stats before retrieval.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we take a K of 25 we run KN&N and we understand we start making connections among very similar documents
takeaways.numbers: K=25; example cluster had 49 chunks at 0.98 average similarity

takeaways.technique: Diversity reranking by community and PageRank
takeaways.what_they_do: After vector retrieval, they rerank results to include documents from different communities and prioritize high-PageRank documents instead of only nearest neighbors.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You can actually use reranking for diversity in your responses.

takeaways.what_they_do: They create weighted co-occurrence relationships among all context documents retrieved for the same query, then analyze which documents come together and how conversations traverse them.
takeaways.evidence_quote: all of these documents that were pulled in by this question will now have a relationship among them

takeaways.technique: Collapse duplicate nodes while preserving lineage
takeaways.what_they_do: They collapse identical text/embedding nodes into one node but keep original relationships so retrieval hits the duplicate once and still traces sources.
takeaways.evidence_quote: collapse them into a single node and we're going to maintain the original relationships
takeaways.numbers: 49 near-identical chunks; one embedding hit instead of 19 or 49

takeaways.what_they_do: They use separate vector indices for subsets such as governance/access boundaries or versions, instead of relying only on metadata filtering inside one index.
takeaways.evidence_quote: certain data that they want available to everybody, certain data they don't, and they manage that from the vector index
